title: Christians of the Middle East
hookLine: the oldest churches, now shrinking; Coptic workers killed in Libya for their faith
last: THE BIBLE READ BY THE POOR.

lines: THE NAME WAS FIRST SPOKEN HERE.
THE WEEK ENDS WHERE IT BEGAN.
cards: "And the disciples were called Christians first in Antioch." That's a line from the book of Acts, and Antioch was a real city in what is now southern Turkey, near the Syrian border.
So the name itself was first spoken in the Middle East. This week traveled the map, to Africa, to Korea, to China, to Latin America.
It ends where the story began, with churches that were never brought in from somewhere else, because they were there from the start.

teach.b: In the early chapters of Acts, followers of Jesus are already in Jerusalem, Damascus and Antioch, long before Paul reaches Rome.
Churches in those lands still trace themselves to that beginning: the Coptic church in Egypt, the Syriac churches, the Assyrian and Chaldean churches of Iraq, the Maronites of Lebanon, the Armenians.
Some still pray in Syriac, a form of Aramaic. Aramaic is the language Mark preserves when Jesus takes a dead girl by the hand.
In the King James Bible: "Talitha cumi; which is, being interpreted, Damsel, I say unto thee, arise." Mark kept the sound of his words, and these churches keep that family of words in their worship.
They aren't a foreign import. They are what was there first.

And in place after place they are fewer than their grandparents knew. War, pressure and poverty have pushed families to leave, and some villages that once filled a church now have few Christian households left.
Some have stayed at great cost.

teach.h: THE MARTYRS ON THE BEACH IN LIBYA.
teach.b: In Libya, a group of Coptic Christian workers, with a man from Ghana among them, were seized by an extremist group and killed for being Christians. Their killers' video was meant to frighten.

Others who watched noticed something else: men on a beach, some praying the name of Jesus as they died. The Coptic Orthodox Church counts them as martyrs, and some of their families said publicly that they forgave.
The oldest churches have carried this a long time, and they are still praying in the old words.

how: The ancient churches of the Middle East celebrate long liturgies in Coptic, Syriac, Arabic and Armenian, and some Christians elsewhere pray for them by name in Sunday prayers.

games.q: Jesus stands beside a girl everyone says is dead. Mark keeps the words he speaks in his own language. what are they?
games.why: "Talitha cumi; which is, being interpreted, Damsel, I say unto thee, arise." Mark kept the Aramaic sound, the language these churches still pray in a form of.

practice: Picture three places: a crowded church in Cairo with incense in the air, a village church on the plain near Mosul that families are coming home to repair, a stone chapel in Syria with Aramaic words carved over the door.
If you pray, pray for Christians in Egypt, Iraq and Syria, and for everyone in those countries who longs for peace; if not, hold each place with good will; people there are praying this hour too.
